questions.question: What are the three types of statements in JDBC?
questions.title: JDBC Statement Types — Statement, PreparedStatement, CallableStatement
questions.direct_answer: JDBC has three statement types: **Statement** (static SQL, no parameters), **PreparedStatement** (parameterized + precompiled, prevents SQL injection — the default choice), and **CallableStatement** (calls stored procedures). All three send SQL; they differ in parameterization and safety.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name the three statement types and when each applies.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defaulting to Statement and building SQL with string concatenation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State PreparedStatement is the default for any SQL with input — safer and faster.

sections.title: The Three JDBC Statement Types
sections.content:
JDBC offers three interfaces for sending SQL:

- **`Statement`** — executes **static** SQL with no parameters. Building it with user input via string concatenation is **unsafe** (SQL injection).
- **`PreparedStatement`** — **parameterized** SQL with `?` placeholders, **precompiled** by the DB, and **injection-safe**. This is the default for any query involving input.
- **`CallableStatement`** — calls **stored procedures** (`{call proc(?, ?)}`), supporting IN/OUT parameters.

`PreparedStatement` extends `Statement`, and `CallableStatement` extends `PreparedStatement`.

sections.title: Statement Types at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|Statement|~static SQL|no parameters|injection risk if concatenated|rare use
emerald|PreparedStatement|~parameterized|? placeholders|precompiled + injection-safe|the default
blue|CallableStatement|~stored procedures|{call proc(?,?)}|IN/OUT params|for DB procedures
amber|Hierarchy|~inheritance|Statement <- PreparedStatement|<- CallableStatement|

sections.title: All three types
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `Statement` with concatenated input**: opens SQL injection — use `PreparedStatement`.
- **Thinking they're unrelated**: they form an inheritance chain.
- **Reaching for `Statement` by habit**: prefer `PreparedStatement` for nearly everything.
- **Using `CallableStatement` for plain queries**: it's for stored procedures.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Statement** — static SQL, no params (risky with input).
- **PreparedStatement** — parameterized, precompiled, injection-safe (default).
- **CallableStatement** — calls stored procedures (IN/OUT params).
- **Inheritance**: Statement ← PreparedStatement ← CallableStatement.
- **Use PreparedStatement** for any SQL with input.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: JDBC gives you three types of statements for sending SQL, and they differ mainly in parameterization and safety. The first is Statement, which executes static SQL with no parameters. The problem is that if you build a Statement by concatenating user input into the SQL string, you open yourself up to SQL injection, so plain Statement is rarely the right choice when input is involved. The second is PreparedStatement, which uses question-mark placeholders for parameters, is precompiled by the database, and is safe against SQL injection because the values are sent separately from the SQL. This is the default I reach for in almost every case. The third is CallableStatement, which is used to call stored procedures, with a syntax like curly-brace call proc with question marks, and it supports both input and output parameters. It's also worth knowing they form an inheritance chain: PreparedStatement extends Statement, and CallableStatement extends PreparedStatement, so each adds capability on top of the previous. So the short version is: Statement for static SQL with no input, PreparedStatement for any parameterized query, which is the safe and fast default, and CallableStatement specifically for stored procedures.

questions.question: Why should you avoid using Statement with string concatenation for user input?
questions.title: SQL Injection Risk with JDBC Statement
questions.direct_answer: Concatenating user input into a `Statement` lets attackers inject SQL — e.g. `' OR '1'='1` turns a login check into 'always true'. **PreparedStatement** with `?` placeholders sends values **separately** from the SQL, so input is treated as data, never executable code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand SQL injection from concatenation and the PreparedStatement fix.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Building SQL by string concatenation and trusting input is harmless.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that parameters are bound as data, so the query structure can't be altered.

sections.title: Why String-Concatenated Statements Are Dangerous
sections.content:
When you build SQL by **concatenating** user input into a `Statement`, the input becomes part of the **executable query**. An attacker can supply `' OR '1'='1` (or `'; DROP TABLE users;--`) and rewrite your query's logic — that's **SQL injection**, a top security risk.

A **PreparedStatement** uses `?` placeholders and **binds values separately** from the SQL text. The database parses the query *first*, then plugs in parameters as **data**, so input can never change the query's structure — no matter what characters it contains.

sections.title: Injection vs Parameterization
sections.content:
rose|Concatenation|~input becomes code|' OR '1'='1|query logic rewritten|SQL injection
emerald|PreparedStatement|~input stays data|? placeholders|bound separately|structure fixed
blue|Why safe|~parse then bind|SQL parsed first|params can't add clauses|special chars harmless
amber|Rule|~never concatenate|input -> always bind|even 'trusted' input|

sections.title: Vulnerable: concatenated Statement
Safe: parameterized PreparedStatement
When This Matters
sections.content:
Any time **user-controlled input** reaches SQL — form fields, query params, headers, file contents — you must parameterize. That's essentially every real query.

Static SQL with **no input** (e.g. `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users`) is safe with a `Statement`, but the moment a value is involved, switch to `PreparedStatement`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Concatenation** makes input part of the executable SQL → injection.
- **`' OR '1'='1`** can turn a check into 'always true'.
- **PreparedStatement** binds values separately as data.
- **The query is parsed first**, so structure can't change.
- **Parameterize** any SQL that touches input.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Concatenating user input into a Statement is dangerous because the input becomes part of the executable SQL, and that's exactly how SQL injection works. Suppose I build a login query by concatenating the username into the SQL string. An attacker enters something like quote space OR space quote one quote equals quote one, and now the WHERE clause becomes name equals empty string OR one equals one, which is always true, so the query returns every user, or worse, an attacker could append a statement that drops a table. The fix is PreparedStatement with question-mark placeholders. Instead of building the SQL with the value inside it, you write the SQL with a placeholder and then bind the value separately using a setter like setString. The crucial difference is timing and separation: the database parses the SQL query first, with the placeholder, and only then plugs in the parameter value as pure data. Because the structure of the query is already fixed before the value arrives, the input can never add new clauses or change the logic, no matter what special characters it contains. So even that classic quote OR one equals one payload is treated as a literal name string and simply doesn't match anyone. The rule I follow is simple: any time user-controlled input reaches SQL, and that's basically every real query, I parameterize with PreparedStatement; I only use a plain Statement for static SQL with no input at all.

questions.question: What is the difference between execute(), executeQuery(), and executeUpdate() in JDBC?
questions.title: execute() vs executeQuery() vs executeUpdate() in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: Use **`executeQuery()`** for SELECT — it returns a `ResultSet`. Use **`executeUpdate()`** for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL — it returns an **int** row count. Use **`execute()`** when you don't know the type ahead of time — it returns a **boolean** (true = a ResultSet is available), and you fetch results accordingly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can match each execute method to the right SQL and return type.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using executeQuery for an UPDATE or vice versa.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note execute() is for dynamic/unknown SQL or statements returning multiple results.

sections.title: execute() vs executeQuery() vs executeUpdate()
sections.content:
Three ways to run SQL, picked by what the statement does and returns:

- **`executeQuery()`** — for **SELECT**; returns a **`ResultSet`** of rows.
- **`executeUpdate()`** — for **INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE** (and DDL); returns an **`int`** = number of affected rows (0 for DDL).
- **`execute()`** — general-purpose for when the SQL type is **unknown** or may return multiple results; returns a **`boolean`** (`true` if the first result is a `ResultSet`), then you call `getResultSet()` / `getUpdateCount()`.

sections.title: Execute Methods at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|executeQuery|~SELECT|returns ResultSet|read rows|never for updates
blue|executeUpdate|~INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE|returns int row count|0 for DDL|never for SELECT
amber|execute|~unknown/dynamic SQL|returns boolean|true = ResultSet|getResultSet/getUpdateCount
rose|Mistake|~wrong method|query for update fails|update for query fails|match to SQL

sections.title: Execute Methods
sections.content:
| Method | For | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `executeQuery()` | SELECT | `ResultSet` |
| `executeUpdate()` | INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL | `int` (rows affected) |
| `execute()` | unknown / multiple results | `boolean` |

sections.title: Wrong method for the SQL
Right method per statement
When to Use Which
sections.content:
Use **`executeQuery`** whenever you're reading data (SELECT). Use **`executeUpdate`** for any write or DDL when you care about how many rows changed.

Use **`execute`** only when you don't know the statement type in advance — dynamic SQL, tools, or procedures that may return a ResultSet *or* an update count (or several).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`executeQuery()`** → SELECT → returns `ResultSet`.
- **`executeUpdate()`** → INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL → returns `int`.
- **`execute()`** → unknown/multiple → returns `boolean`.
- **Match the method** to the SQL or it fails.
- **`execute`** is for dynamic SQL and mixed results.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: JDBC gives you three execute methods, and you pick based on what the SQL does and what you want back. executeQuery is for SELECT statements; it returns a ResultSet that you iterate over to read rows. executeUpdate is for data-changing statements, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE, as well as DDL like CREATE; it returns an int, the number of rows affected, which is zero for DDL. And execute is the general-purpose one, used when you don't know the statement type ahead of time or it might return multiple results; it returns a boolean, where true means the first result is a ResultSet, and then you call getResultSet or getUpdateCount to retrieve the actual results. The mistakes to avoid are mixing them up: calling executeQuery on an update, or executeUpdate on a select, is wrong because the return types don't match the operation. In day-to-day code I'm almost always using executeQuery for reads and executeUpdate for writes, and I rarely need the generic execute. The execute method really comes into play in things like database tools, dynamically generated SQL where you genuinely don't know if it's a query or an update, or stored procedures that can return a ResultSet or an update count, sometimes several in sequence.

questions.question: When would you use a Statement instead of PreparedStatement?
questions.title: When to Use Statement vs PreparedStatement
questions.direct_answer: Use a plain **Statement** only for **static SQL with no parameters** that runs **once** — like one-off DDL (`CREATE TABLE`), admin/migration scripts, or simple constant queries. The moment any user input or repetition is involved, switch to **PreparedStatement** for safety and performance.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the narrow legitimate uses of Statement.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Statement for parameterized or repeated queries.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note Statement avoids the precompile overhead for truly one-off static SQL.

sections.title: When a Plain Statement Is Acceptable
sections.content:
`PreparedStatement` is the default, but a plain **`Statement`** is fine in a few narrow cases: **static SQL with no input** that you run **once**. Examples:

- **One-off DDL** — `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE` in a migration.
- **Admin/maintenance scripts** — fixed queries with no parameters.
- **Constant queries** — `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users` with no variable parts.

For a single execution of fixed SQL, `Statement` skips the precompile setup. But add **any** parameter or run it **repeatedly**, and `PreparedStatement` wins on both **safety** and **performance**.

sections.title: When to Use Statement
sections.content:
emerald|OK for|~static, one-off|DDL: CREATE/ALTER|admin scripts|constant queries
rose|Not for|~input or repetition|user-supplied values|loops/batches|use PreparedStatement
blue|Why OK|~no params|nothing to inject|run-once|no precompile benefit lost
amber|Switch when|~any variable|input present|executed many times|safety + speed

sections.title: Statement for one-off DDL; PreparedStatement otherwise
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Statement with input**: any user value → injection risk; parameterize.
- **Statement in a loop**: repeated parsing wastes time — PreparedStatement is precompiled.
- **Over-thinking it**: for fixed one-off DDL, Statement is perfectly fine.
- **Assuming Statement is always faster**: only for true single-run static SQL.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Statement** suits static, parameterless, run-once SQL.
- **Good for** one-off DDL and admin scripts.
- **Avoid** Statement with input or in loops.
- **PreparedStatement** wins on safety and on repeated execution.
- **Default to PreparedStatement** unless it's clearly static one-off SQL.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Even though PreparedStatement is the default, there are a few narrow situations where a plain Statement is perfectly acceptable, and the common thread is static SQL with no parameters that you run once. The clearest example is one-off DDL, like a CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE in a migration script; there's no user input and you run it a single time, so a Statement is fine. The same goes for admin or maintenance scripts with fixed queries, or a constant query like SELECT COUNT star FROM users that has no variable parts. In those cases a Statement actually avoids the small overhead of precompiling that a PreparedStatement sets up, since you're only running the SQL once. But the moment any of two things is true, I switch to PreparedStatement. The first is user input: if any value comes from outside, concatenating it into a Statement risks SQL injection, so it must be parameterized. The second is repetition: if you're running the same query many times, say in a loop or a batch, a PreparedStatement is precompiled once and reused, so it's faster, whereas a Statement re-parses every time. So my rule is to default to PreparedStatement and only fall back to Statement for clearly static, parameterless, run-once SQL like DDL.

questions.question: What is the performance benefit of PreparedStatement over Statement?
questions.title: PreparedStatement Performance Benefits
questions.direct_answer: **PreparedStatement** is faster for repeated execution because the database **parses and builds the execution plan once** (precompiles), then reuses it for every call with new parameters. A plain **Statement** re-parses and re-plans the SQL on **every** execution, wasting work in loops and batches.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know PreparedStatement amortizes parsing/planning via precompilation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking PreparedStatement is only about security, not performance.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention server-side statement caching and batch execution amplifying the gain.

sections.title: Why PreparedStatement Is Faster
sections.content:
Running SQL involves **parsing** it, **planning** an execution strategy, and then executing. A plain `Statement` redoes **parse + plan on every call** — fine once, wasteful in a loop. A **`PreparedStatement`** is **precompiled**: the database parses and plans it **once** (often caching the plan), then each execution just **rebinds parameters** and runs.

For a query run many times — inserting 10,000 rows, a per-request lookup — this reuse plus **batching** makes `PreparedStatement` significantly faster, on top of its injection safety.

sections.title: PreparedStatement Performance
sections.content:
rose|Statement|~re-parse each call|parse + plan every time|wasteful in loops|no reuse
emerald|PreparedStatement|~precompiled|parse + plan once|rebind params + run|cached plan
amber|Batching|~amplifies gain|addBatch/executeBatch|fewer round-trips|big bulk speedup
blue|Bonus|~also safer|injection-safe|two wins in one|the default

sections.title: Statement in a loop — re-parsed every time
PreparedStatement + batch — compiled once
When the Speedup Matters Most
sections.content:
The gain is biggest for **repeated execution**: bulk inserts/updates, queries run per request at high volume, and anything you can **batch**. For a single one-off query the difference is negligible.

Since `PreparedStatement` also prevents injection, it's the right default even when performance isn't the main concern.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **PreparedStatement precompiles** — parse + plan once, reuse.
- **Statement re-parses/re-plans** on every execution.
- **Biggest win** in loops, bulk ops, and high-volume queries.
- **Batching** (`addBatch`/`executeBatch`) multiplies the gain.
- **Also injection-safe** — two benefits in one.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: People often think PreparedStatement is only about security, but it's also a real performance win, and the reason is precompilation. Whenever the database runs SQL, it has to parse the text, build an execution plan, and then execute. A plain Statement redoes the parsing and planning on every single call. That's fine if you run it once, but if you're running the same query in a loop, you're paying that parse-and-plan cost over and over. A PreparedStatement, by contrast, is precompiled: the database parses and plans it once, often caching the plan, and then each execution just rebinds the new parameter values and runs. So for something like inserting ten thousand rows, or a lookup query that runs on every request at high volume, the reuse adds up to a significant speedup. And you can amplify it further with batching, where you queue many parameter sets with addBatch and send them all at once with executeBatch, which dramatically cuts the number of network round-trips. For a single one-off query the difference is negligible, so this matters most for repeated execution. The nice thing is you don't have to choose between safety and speed, because PreparedStatement gives you both: it prevents SQL injection and it's faster for repeated queries, which is why it's the sensible default.

questions.question: What is CallableStatement in JDBC and when do you use it?
questions.title: CallableStatement in JDBC — Stored Procedures
questions.direct_answer: A **CallableStatement** is the JDBC interface for invoking **stored procedures** and functions in the database, using the `{call proc_name(?, ?)}` escape syntax. It supports **IN**, **OUT**, and **INOUT** parameters — you register OUT params with `registerOutParameter` and read them after execution.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know CallableStatement calls stored procedures with IN/OUT parameters.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to register OUT parameters before reading them.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain when stored procedures are worth it (DB-side logic) vs keeping logic in the app.

sections.title: What CallableStatement Is For
sections.content:
**`CallableStatement`** (a subtype of `PreparedStatement`) calls **stored procedures** — reusable SQL routines stored in the database. You create one with `con.prepareCall("{call proc(?, ?)}")` using the JDBC **escape syntax**.

Procedures can have three parameter directions: **IN** (input you set), **OUT** (output the procedure returns), and **INOUT** (both). You must **`registerOutParameter`** for each OUT param *before* executing, then read it afterward. Use stored procedures when logic genuinely belongs in the DB; otherwise keep logic in the application.

sections.title: CallableStatement at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~calls stored procedures|prepareCall|{call proc(?,?)}|subtype of PreparedStatement
emerald|Params|~three directions|IN you set|OUT you read|INOUT both
amber|OUT params|~must register|registerOutParameter|before execute|read after
rose|When|~DB-side logic|reuse across apps|heavy data ops|else keep logic in app

sections.title: Steps to Call a Procedure
sections.content:
| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | `con.prepareCall("{call proc(?, ?)}")` |
| 2 | set IN params (`setInt`, `setString`) |
| 3 | `registerOutParameter(idx, Types.X)` for OUT params |
| 4 | `execute()` |
| 5 | read OUT params (`getInt`, `getString`) |

sections.title: Calling a procedure with an OUT parameter
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not registering OUT params**: reading them without `registerOutParameter` fails.
- **Wrong parameter index/type**: indices are 1-based and types must match.
- **Overusing stored procedures**: business logic hidden in the DB is harder to test/version.
- **Using `Statement` for procedures**: use `CallableStatement` and the `{call ...}` syntax.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **CallableStatement** calls stored procedures/functions.
- **Escape syntax**: `{call proc(?, ?)}` via `prepareCall`.
- **IN / OUT / INOUT** parameter directions.
- **Register OUT params** before executing; read them after.
- **Use procedures** for DB-side logic, not as a default.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: CallableStatement is the JDBC interface you use to call stored procedures and functions that live inside the database. It's actually a subtype of PreparedStatement, and you create one with connection dot prepareCall, passing the JDBC escape syntax, which looks like curly brace call, the procedure name, and question marks for the parameters. The thing that makes CallableStatement special is parameter directions. A procedure can have IN parameters, which are inputs you set like a normal PreparedStatement, OUT parameters, which are values the procedure returns to you, and INOUT parameters that do both. For any OUT parameter, you have to call registerOutParameter with its index and SQL type before you execute, and then after execution you read it with the matching getter like getInt. So the typical flow is: prepareCall, set your IN parameters, register your OUT parameters, call execute, and then read the OUT values. A common mistake is forgetting to register the OUT parameters, which causes a failure when you try to read them, and remembering that parameter indices are one-based. On the design side, stored procedures are worth using when the logic genuinely belongs in the database, like heavy data operations or logic shared across multiple applications, but I'm cautious about putting too much business logic in procedures, because it's harder to test and version-control than application code.

questions.question: How does PreparedStatement's precompilation improve performance?
questions.title: PreparedStatement Precompilation and Performance
questions.direct_answer: **Precompilation** means the database parses the SQL, validates it, and builds an **execution plan once** when the `PreparedStatement` is prepared. Each execution then skips straight to **binding parameters and running** the cached plan — avoiding repeated parse/optimize work, which is the performance gain for repeated queries.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can explain what precompilation actually does step by step.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'it's compiled' without explaining parse/plan reuse.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish client-side prepare from server-side prepared statements/plan caching.

sections.title: How Precompilation Improves Performance
sections.content:
When a `PreparedStatement` is prepared, the database does the expensive one-time work up front: **parse** the SQL (syntax check), **validate** it (tables/columns exist), and **build an execution plan** (how to fetch the data). This compiled form is **cached**.

On each `execute`, the database **skips parse/plan** and goes straight to **binding the parameter values** and running the cached plan. So the parse-and-optimize cost is paid **once** and amortized across many executions — a big win for queries run repeatedly.

sections.title: Precompilation at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Prepare phase|~one-time cost|parse SQL|validate tables/columns|build execution plan
emerald|Execute phase|~cheap, repeated|bind parameters|run cached plan|skip parse/plan
amber|Net effect|~amortized cost|pay parse once|reuse many times|fast in loops
rose|Server-side|~real prepared stmt|plan cached in DB|vs client-side prepare|depends on driver/DB

sections.title: Prepare once, execute many
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Re-preparing inside the loop**: defeats the purpose — prepare once, execute many.
- **Saying 'compiled to machine code'**: it's parse + plan caching, not native compilation.
- **Assuming all DBs cache server-side identically**: some prepare client-side; behaviour varies.
- **Expecting a gain for a single run**: precompilation pays off with repetition.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Prepare** = parse + validate + build execution plan, once.
- **Execute** = bind parameters + run the cached plan.
- **Parse/optimize cost** is paid once, reused many times.
- **Prepare once, execute many** — don't re-prepare in a loop.
- **Server-side vs client-side** prepare varies by driver/DB.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Precompilation is what makes a PreparedStatement faster for repeated queries, so it helps to walk through what actually happens. When you prepare a PreparedStatement, the database does the expensive work up front and just once: it parses the SQL to check the syntax, validates it by confirming the tables and columns exist, and builds an execution plan, which is the strategy for how it'll fetch the data, like which index to use. That compiled, planned form gets cached. Then, on each execution, the database skips the parsing and planning entirely and goes straight to binding your parameter values into the placeholders and running the cached plan. So the costly parse-and-optimize step is paid once and then amortized across every execution. That's why running the same query many times, say looking up orders for a list of customer ids, is much faster with a PreparedStatement: it's parsed and planned once and reused for each id. A couple of clarifications I'd add. This is not compilation to machine code; it's parsing and plan caching. And the exact behaviour depends on the driver and database: some do a true server-side prepared statement where the plan is cached in the database, while others prepare more on the client side. The practical takeaway is to prepare once outside your loop and execute many times inside it, rather than re-preparing each iteration.

questions.question: How do you execute a stored procedure with JDBC?
questions.title: Executing Stored Procedures in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: To run a stored procedure in JDBC, use a **CallableStatement** created with `con.prepareCall("{call proc(?, ?)}")`: set the IN parameters, **register any OUT parameters** with `registerOutParameter`, call **execute()**, then read OUT params or the returned `ResultSet`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the CallableStatement workflow for stored procedures.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a regular Statement, or skipping registerOutParameter for OUT params.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Handle procedures that return a ResultSet vs OUT params, and close resources.

sections.title: Executing a Stored Procedure
sections.content:
Stored procedures are called through a **`CallableStatement`** using the JDBC escape syntax `{call proc_name(?, ?)}`. The recipe:

1. **`prepareCall`** with the `{call ...}` syntax.
2. **Set IN params** (`setInt`, `setString`).
3. **Register OUT params** (`registerOutParameter(idx, Types.X)`) — required before reading them.
4. **`execute()`** (or `executeQuery()` if it returns a result set).
5. **Read results** — OUT params via getters, or iterate the returned `ResultSet`.

Wrap it in try-with-resources so the statement closes.

sections.title: Stored Procedure Call at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|prepareCall|~start|{call proc(?,?)}|CallableStatement|escape syntax
emerald|IN params|~inputs|setInt/setString|by 1-based index|like PreparedStatement
amber|OUT params|~register first|registerOutParameter|before execute|read after with getXxx
rose|Results|~two shapes|OUT params|or a ResultSet|handle both

sections.title: The Recipe
sections.content:
| Step | Code |
|---|---|
| 1 | `con.prepareCall("{call proc(?, ?)}")` |
| 2 | `cs.setString(1, ...)` |
| 3 | `cs.registerOutParameter(2, Types.INTEGER)` |
| 4 | `cs.execute()` |
| 5 | `cs.getInt(2)` or iterate `ResultSet` |

sections.title: Procedure returning an OUT param and a ResultSet
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `Statement`/`PreparedStatement`**: procedures need `CallableStatement` + `{call ...}`.
- **Skipping `registerOutParameter`**: OUT values can't be read without it.
- **Wrong index/type**: 1-based indices; OUT type must match the procedure.
- **Not closing**: wrap in try-with-resources to release the statement.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Use `CallableStatement`** with `{call proc(?, ?)}`.
- **Set IN params**, then **register OUT params** before execute.
- **`execute()`** runs it; OUT params read afterward.
- **Procedures may return** a ResultSet, OUT params, or both.
- **try-with-resources** to close the statement.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: To execute a stored procedure in JDBC you use a CallableStatement, which you create with connection dot prepareCall, passing the JDBC escape syntax that looks like curly brace call, the procedure name, and question marks for the parameters. The workflow is a clear recipe. First, prepareCall with that call syntax. Second, set your IN parameters using the same setters as a PreparedStatement, like setInt or setString, with one-based indices. Third, and this is the step people forget, register any OUT parameters with registerOutParameter, giving the parameter index and its SQL type, and you must do this before executing. Fourth, call execute, or executeQuery if the procedure returns a result set. Fifth, read the results: you read OUT parameters with the matching getters like getInt after execution, and if the procedure returns rows you iterate the ResultSet. One nuance is that procedures can return different shapes: some return OUT parameters, some return a ResultSet, and some return both, so you handle whichever applies, often checking the boolean from execute to see if a ResultSet is available. As always, I wrap the CallableStatement in try-with-resources so it's closed properly. The main mistakes to avoid are trying to call a procedure with a plain Statement, forgetting to register the OUT parameters, and mismatching the parameter index or type.
